title: Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents
abstract: Long coding agent sessions outgrow the model's context window, so agents compact: older history is replaced by something shorter, usually a model-written summary. A summary selects and rewords, and the agent cannot see what was lost. Existing work has explored a range of compaction techniques, but comparatively little attention has been paid to their effectiveness with lightweight models, including those deployed locally or used for high-volume workloads. Here, we present transparent-compact, a simple deterministic method for the open-source Pi coding agent, designed specifically for use with such models and with the purpose of maximising the transparency of the agent's view of its own compacted context. It guarantees that user and assistant prose in its context is unchanged by a model or algorithm, and explicitly flags where compaction has stripped information. We compare it with Pi's default model-written summary compaction and with pi-vcc, a popular deterministic method with similar methods but without verbatim retention of prose. Our benchmarks run on four models of varying performance levels, with emphasis on Qwen3.8-27B: a lightweight model at the top end of what consumer hardware can serve locally. On sets probing commitments (rules the user set which exist only in the conversation) and recall of facts, transparent-compact matched or outperformed both alternatives. In particular, it showed an advantage in avoiding confident blunders, i.e. assertion of false information as opposed to recognizing that something was not recalled. Even with a frontier model, its advantage was present but smaller. We argue that transparent-compact spares lightweight models from reasoning or searching their way around what compaction lost, and results in improved recall and application of information as a result, without the need for task or context-specific structuring of the session history.

title: VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) and queried sparsely within the inverse-rendering objectives, while the original 3DGS loop is retained for training efficiency, interactive visualization, and tooling compatibility. Shading follows a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation with a principled microfacet bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) and low-resolution high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps. We evaluate our method on the TensoIR synthetic dataset against baselines based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), tensor representations, and 3DGS. The results show competitive performance and improvements over several earlier baselines for novel-view synthesis (NVS), albedo reconstruction, and relighting. Ablations indicate that explicit visibility modeling is an important contributor to relighting and material-illumination disentanglement, while pure PBR supervision can favor appearance fitting in NVS. Overall, the findings suggest that sparse, point-based visibility queries effectively complement rasterized splatting for inverse rendering while preserving the practical advantages of the 3DGS ecosystem.

title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.

We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.

title: W-JEPA: Wavelet Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Wearable Activity Recognition
abstract: A major challenge in wearable device activity recognition is the heterogeneity across datasets in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate and subjects. Moreover, the motion patterns that distinguish activities often appear as subtle, scale-specific variations within otherwise similar waveforms. As a result, raw signals are often ambiguous, and models trained on them tend to rely on cues specific to a particular sensor setup or participant, which limits both cross-dataset transfer and generalization to unseen participants. Addressing this requires representations that preserve such activity-relevant, scale-specific variation. We introduce W-JEPA, a self-supervised framework that exploits the multiscale structure of inertial motion and leverages a joint-embedding predictive architecture, by organizing windows into a fixed grid of wavelet tokens indexed by scale, sensor axis, and time. These wavelet tokens help expose activity-specific detail within broadly similar raw signals, and serve as the units of masked latent prediction. W-JEPA predicts masked token representations supplied by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder. Because recovering a masked token requires relating motion at one scale and axis to motion at other scales and axes, the model learns the cross-scale, cross-axis structure of human movement. Across six wearable activity benchmarks, W-JEPA outperforms state-of-the-art methods under random-window splits and remains the strongest when subjects are held out, improving average macro-F1 by 8.7 percentage points over the strongest published baseline. These results indicate that physically grounded multiscale tokenization, combined together with latent predictive learning, provides a promising foundation for transferable representations of heterogeneous wearable inertial data.

title: Data Curation and Model Souping: Unlocking Qwen3-0.6B for MS MARCO Passage Ranking
abstract: This report studies passage retrieval and re-ranking on the MS MARCO benchmark using lightweight Qwen3-0.6B models. Across three experimental settings --- BM25-then-reranking task, corpus-wide dense retrieval task, and dense retrieval then re-ranking task --- the results demonstrate that competitive ranking performance can be achieved without complex architectural modifications, custom loss functions, or cross-encoder distillation. Instead, substantial gains stem from data-centric strategies: corpus-targeted continued pre-training, rigorous data curation, hard-negative mining, training--inference distribution alignment, and weight merging via Model Soup. In particular, Model Soup delivers marked performance gains while preserving the inference efficiency of a single model. These findings highlight how data curation and weight merging can push sub-billion-parameter models to state-of-the-art performance. My models can be downloaded from Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/shuguangh/models

title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
abstract: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.

title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
abstract: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.

title: A preregistered frame-only census of game mechanics, fitted on ARC-AGI-3, failed its validity test on MiniGrid/BabyAI and Procgen
abstract: Before any confirmatory run, I registered the claim that a fixed battery of frame-only probes, the assumption census, would report five mechanical assumptions of unseen games as each game’s source code states them. It would also predict on which games assumptiondriven frame-only agents complete the first level. I froze every census parameter on eight ARC-AGI-3 games. Test V1 compared the census with source-derived truth tables; test V2 compared a census score with first-level completion by three agents. The census and the agents ran on 161 MiniGrid/BabyAI environments under two action conditions and on 14 Procgen games under two camera settings, with 10 seeds and 20,000 actions per run, 10,500 runs in all. By the registered outcome table the result is a refutation, under the clause “V1 fails on any suite”. V1 failed for three of five assumptions under absolute moves and for four of five under primitive actions on MiniGrid/BabyAI, and for four of five on Procgen. No agent passed V2 on any suite. On all six primary MiniGrid/BabyAI lines, a nuisance baseline built from grid area, action count and color count ranked the games better than the census did. An exploratory reading made after the outcome suggests that for four of the five assumptions the probes and the truth definitions were not the same construct. The lesson is procedural: check an instrument against known truth where its parameters are set, and on the pilot games, before any confirmatory use.

title: CCM: Relationstypen und Interpretationswechsel. Band 2
abstract: CCM Band 2 enthält 200 deutsch-englische Arbeitsdefinitionen zu Relationstypen und begrenzten Interpretationswechseln. Alle Einträge sind Bereichsfestlegungen. Beispiele, Gegenfälle und Grenzen stehen auf Deutsch. Zehn Module behandeln Relationen, Funktionen, Beobachtungsbedingungen, Quotienten, Relationsoperationen, endliche Prüfungen, Symbolinterpretation, Zustandsoperationen, Vergleichsbelege und Ausgabegrenzen. Bekannte Mathematik wird nicht als historische Erfindung ausgegeben. KI-unterstützte redaktionelle Arbeitsfassung; keine bestätigte Disziplingründung, unabhängige Fachbegutachtung oder empirische Wirkung. Volume 2 contains 200 paired German-English scoped working definitions. Original finite Python cases use four synthetic topic/status states. Topic projection preserves a topic-only predicate but cannot exactly recover the erased status predicate. A status flip admits a representative-independent topic-class operation; a status-dependent topic assignment does not. Two fixed operation orders differ. A three-state chain distinguishes original pairs from a computed transitive closure. Empty-relation reflexivity differs between an empty and a nonempty carrier. These are exact finite models, not an RDF processor, free-text comprehension, a theorem prover, subjective experience or empirical cognitive-continuity evidence. Same-assistant standalone rerun produced identical result bytes; shared errors remain possible. Six files: PDF, TXT, definitions JSON, references JSON, original Python and computed result JSON. PDF/TXT contain the same text. Selected Hammack and RDF 1.1 Semantics passages are bounded mathematical/contextual sources; no textbook wording, figures, tasks, code or W3C examples reproduced. Own prior works are not independent validation. 123 conservative core links leave 77 additional editorial core concepts relative to preceding main and locally prepared inventories. Grouped closure-operation and exhaustive-test families do not assert that the different closures or tested laws are mathematically identical. Publication order requires preserving prepared-core overlap. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 applies only to available rights; sources and font components retain rights. No general public adapted/translated redistribution licensed. No professional legal or translation clearance. A later DOI would provide archival identity, not peer review or immunity from criticism.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Parallel-World Self-Verification and Cross-Verification for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate plausible but incorrect answers, and their ability to verify their own outputs does not necessarily improve in proportion to their generation capabilities. Existing approaches investigate self-verification, self-consistency, multi-agent debate, and cross-model evaluation. However, verification systems can remain inefficient when they rely on a fixed verification pathway or use additional models without explicitly determining when independent verification is necessary. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Self-Verification and Cross-Verification (APSCV), a conceptual framework that dynamically switches between self-verification and cross-verification for multiple large language models. The framework introduces parallel verification worlds, defined as multiple verification branches generated by the same underlying model but assigned different verification objectives, perspectives, or strategies. These branches can verify their own judgments, cross-verify one another, or collaborate with heterogeneous external models. A verification controller selects the next operation according to disagreement, estimated uncertainty, historical verifier reliability, evidence availability, task risk, and computational cost. The framework further incorporates selective escalation, evidence-aware aggregation, and a stopping mechanism intended to prevent unnecessary verification cycles. The proposed approach is formalized as a sequential decision-making problem and accompanied by an implementable algorithm, research questions, testable hypotheses, and an experimental evaluation protocol. Its central proposition is that verification should be treated as an adaptive process rather than a fixed sequence of model calls. The framework is a research proposal; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing systems require empirical evaluation and further literature review.

title: Testing graph isomorphism using simple quantum circuits
abstract: The graph isomorphism problem asks whether two graphs are equivalent up to a permutation of their vertices. Its precise computational complexity remains unresolved, and it is still unknown whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists. We investigate whether simple graph-dependent Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) and Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) circuits can distinguish non-isomorphic graphs. We first show that suitable IQP and QAOA constructions allow the underlying graph to be reconstructed using a polynomial number of samples. Building on previous work using the QAOA energy, we show that Hamming weight distributions can distinguish graph pairs at circuit depths for which the numerically computed energy gap is zero. We then apply graph invariants to the matrix of ZZ correlators on the output distribution. For the specific case of the graph spectrum, at QAOA depth $p=2$, this invariant numerically distinguishes all $10{,}486$ cospectral regular graph pairs tested on up to 18 vertices. For IQP circuits, we introduce a finer invariant based on probability multiplicities within Hamming weight sectors, which distinguishes every non-isomorphic graph pair tested numerically. Finally, we derive exact graph-theoretic characterisations of the IQP output distribution at $θ=π/2$ and $θ=π/4$. These results show that simple graph-dependent quantum circuits encode substantial structural information, while leaving open whether this information can be extracted efficiently for general graph isomorphism.

title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $α$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $α=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $α$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $α=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning
abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, updating shared parameters when learning new tasks often overwrites existing knowledge, causing catastrophic forgetting. Memory replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting but rely on previous samples, raising privacy, memory, and scalability concerns. On the other hand, parameter isolation-based methods preserve learned knowledge but may limit knowledge transfer, whereas regularization promotes adaptability but remains susceptible to interference between old and new tasks. To maintain the stability-plasticity trade-off, this paper proposes Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection (SPARS), a replay-free hybrid framework combining global parameter isolation with localized parameter regularization. SPARS estimates parameter importance using either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a novel Confidence Score (CS) estimator that leverages logit sensitivity and achieves comparable performance to FIM without requiring labelled data. Based on parameter importance, SPARS partitions parameters into three importance-aware regions namely, winning, neighboring, and non-important parameter regions. Each region receives a different adaptation strategy: selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning based on its role in the stability-plasticity trade-off. To mitigate classifier bias in class-incremental learning, we employ Quadratic Discriminant Analysis to improve performance on previously learned classes .Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate consistent improvement in average incremental accuracy over existing isolation- and regularization-based methods across task- and class-incremental learning. On TinyImageNet, SPARS achieves the best performance with 6% improvement for class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.

title: Continual pretraining Prostate MRI ViT Encoder for task alignment
abstract: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.

title: MultiPartyTurnBench: Benchmarking Floor Control in Multi-Party Spoken Dialogue
abstract: Full-duplex speech systems must decide when to enter, hold, or relinquish the conversational floor, even as multiple speakers overlap or backchannel without taking it. Existing evaluations study dyadic turn-taking or end-to-end agent behavior, but lack a unified, controlled evaluation of genuine floor transitions against confusable non-events in multi-party settings. We introduce MultiPartyTurnBench (MPTB), a benchmark of 240 synthetically generated, channel-separated conversations spanning two to five speakers and six interaction types. MPTB evaluates two complementary tasks: End-of-Turn (EOT) detection distinguishes genuine turn completion from temporary holds, while Interruption (INT) detection distinguishes successful floor takeovers from non-floor-taking speech. Exact event-conditioned annotations enable causal evaluation using false-positive-constrained recall and signed latency. Across acoustic, semantic, and turn-projection baselines, we find a stark asymmetry: learned systems achieve 82.5-92.6% EOT recall at 4.3-11.8% false-positive rates, while INT detection suffers from missed takeovers or excessive false activations. This asymmetry extends to five full-duplex agents which achieve 86.1-95.8% balanced accuracy on turn entry, yet perform near chance (46.9-54.7%) on selective interruption handling. Gemini-3.8-Live yields to 97.7% of backchannels, whereas MiniCPM-o-4.5 yields to only 1.4% of genuine interruptions. These findings establish selective floor control as a distinct, unresolved challenge for reliable multi-party voice interaction.

title: MIPS: Mitigating Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning for Large Outcome Spaces
abstract: Expected-reward maximization in reinforcement learning concentrates probability mass on a few outcomes, even in tasks that require many distinct, high-quality solutions, a failure known as mode collapse. Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) counters this in group-based policy gradients such as GRPO by dividing each reward by the outcome's probability, estimated from its frequency within the sampled group. When the outcome space is large relative to the group, outcomes rarely repeat and these estimates become uninformative. Since an outcome can be constructed along many trajectories, its probability is a sum over all of them, and computing it directly is intractable. We propose Marginal IPS (MIPS), which performs marginal evaluation by combining the sampled trajectory with a learned model of the trajectories that lead to each outcome. On Hypergrids, where the exact sampling distribution is computable, MIPS stays near the reward-distribution target as the outcome space grows relative to the rollout group, while frequency-based IPS degrades. In molecular synthesis and phylogenetic inference, MIPS sustains diverse, high-quality sampling where GRPO and frequency-based IPS collapse, showing that MIPS serves as a reliable solution to mode collapse in RL.

title: IMU-Bench: Benchmarking Wrist IMU Representations Across Kinematic, Semantic and Clinical Tasks
abstract: Wrist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a common sensing modality for tasks ranging from activity and gesture recognition to pose estimation, inertial odometry and clinical motor assessment. Existing wearable benchmarks evaluate performance across multiple tasks, but leave open how supervision for one task affects transfer to others and whether these tasks benefit from a shared representation. We present IMU-Bench, a benchmark of ten tasks from eight datasets for studying IMU multi-task performance and cross-task transfer. We compare six self-supervised methods pretrained on unlabeled recorded and simulated wrist motion, evaluating classification, pose and velocity estimation, and IMU-language retrieval. We find that our masked autoencoder, InrtlWrist, achieves the best or joint-best frozen-probe performance on nine of ten tasks, and fine-tuning improves on training from scratch on nine of ten tasks, including full-body pose, odometry and retrieval. Across transfer and joint-training experiments, supervision that benefits one target can reduce performance on others, with supervised sources transferring within kinematic estimation while, under frozen probing, none approaches the pretrained encoder on language retrieval, and joint-training gains that come at a cost to the paired task. These findings distinguish broad downstream usefulness from complementary task supervision. Code, task cards and a leaderboard are publicly available.

title: Denoising Score Matching in Diffusion Models: The Effect of Rank Constraints on Generalization
abstract: Architectural biases restrict the class of functions that a diffusion score network can represent, but their effect on generalization remains poorly understood. We study denoising score matching with score networks having a rank constrained non-linear term and a linear skip connection. Numerical experiments with trainable three-layer networks on data supported on an embedded sphere show that increasing rank lowers training error, but its effect on test error depends on sample size and data dimension. To explain this behavior, we analyze a random-feature score model under rank constraint with Gaussian data supported on a low-dimensional subspace. We characterize the optimal rank-constrained estimator through a truncated singular value decomposition and derive asymptotically precise limiting training and test errors when sample size $(n)$, feature width $(p)$, data dimension $(D)$, and rank $(r)$ scale proportionally with the ambient dimension $(d)$. The resulting spectral characterization distinguishes eigenmodes that improve the empirical fit from those that improve population accuracy. It also identifies the dimension of the orthogonal complement of the data subspace as a natural rank threshold. The theoretical learning curves qualitatively reproduce the observed rank-dependent overfitting, providing a tractable account of how bottlenecks or rank constraints can regularize score estimation and why their effectiveness depends on data dimension and sample size.

title: Artificial Intelligence Needs Control Theory: Towards Stable, Adaptive, and Autonomous AI Systems
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly capable of reasoning, planning, and interacting with external tools. However, capability alone does not guarantee stable behavior, reliable execution, or successful task completion under uncertainty and disturbances. This paper investigates how control-theoretic principles can inform the design of more stable, adaptive, and autonomous AI systems. It develops a formal model of the closed cognitive control loop, examines practical stability and actuator gain uncertainty, and introduces the Unified Cognitive Control Framework (UCCF), a proposed architecture integrating state estimation, feedback, adaptation, verification, and safety mechanisms. The framework is evaluated through a simulation-based proof of concept using a controlled navigation task. Across 500 trials per configuration, the full UCCF configuration achieved an 83.8% task success rate, compared with 61.4% for a raw-feedback baseline. These results provide preliminary evidence that combining feedback with additional control and verification mechanisms can improve task performance in the simulated environment. The study also discusses limitations concerning metric validation, model assumptions, computational overhead, and generalization to deployed AI agents. The simulation does not establish equivalent performance improvements in real-world large language model (LLM) agents. This work contributes a control-oriented perspective on autonomous AI system design and outlines a research direction for integrating stability, adaptation, and runtime verification into increasingly capable AI architectures. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Control Theory; Autonomous Systems; LLM Agents; Feedback Control; Runtime Verification; Stability; Adaptive Systems. Author: Mohamed EidAffiliation: OpenQCore AI Research

title: XpliCAI goes beyond guidelines: transparent to whom, and for what?
abstract: This poster presents the XpliCAI project, a participatory initiative conducted at Geneva University Hospitals (HUG) to co-develop an operational framework for AI transparency in healthcare. Based on six workshops involving healthcare professionals, patient partners, caregivers, and hospital staff, the project identified and prioritized transparency requirements for clinical AI systems. The resulting framework includes 20 indicators addressing explainability, human oversight, governance, traceability, and accountability, together with practical recommendations for implementation.

title: A Dual-Strategy Cuckoo Catfish Optimizer for Continuous Optimization with Application to Wastewater Treatment
abstract: Candidate generation in population-based optimization depends on both the starting population and the information exchanged during search. This study proposes the dual-strategy enhanced cuckoo catfish optimizer (DCCO), which modifies these two stages within the cuckoo catfish optimizer (CCO). Clustering-based Cauchy sampling generates approximately half of the initial population around geometric reference centers, while uniform sampling supplies the remainder. Horizontal and normalized-coordinate vertical crossover then recombine individuals and coordinates after each CCO population sweep. On 29 CEC2017 functions at D=30, DCCO achieves an average rank of 1.7586, the lowest among the nine compared methods. Component comparisons and parameter analysis characterize the integrated configuration. In a static wastewater operational model, the mean operating cost index is 22.63% and 24.64% lower than that of the swift flight optimizer (SFO) and CCO, respectively, under dry conditions. The selected decisions remain feasible under dry and rain loads, while all violate the storm constraints, motivating scenario-constrained decisions. The study evaluates the quality–computation trade-off of the integrated search design and its cost–feasibility behavior within the stated algebraic model.

evidence.title: A Dual-Strategy Cuckoo Catfish Optimizer for Continuous Optimization with Application to Wastewater Treatment
evidence.abstract: Candidate generation in population-based optimization depends on both the starting population and the information exchanged during search. This study proposes the dual-strategy enhanced cuckoo catfish optimizer (DCCO), which modifies these two stages within the cuckoo catfish optimizer (CCO). Clustering-based Cauchy sampling generates approximately half of the initial population around geometric reference centers, while uniform sampling supplies the remainder. Horizontal and normalized-coordinate vertical crossover then recombine individuals and coordinates after each CCO population sweep. On 29 CEC2017 functions at D=30, DCCO achieves an average rank of 1.7586, the lowest among the nine compared methods. Component comparisons and parameter analysis characterize the integrated configuration. In a static wastewater operational model, the mean operating cost index is 22.63% and 24.64% lower than that of the swift flight optimizer (SFO) and CCO, respectively, under dry conditions. The selected decisions remain feasible under dry and rain loads, while all violate the storm constraints, motivating scenario-constrained decisions. The study evaluates the quality–computation trade-off of the integrated search design and its cost–feasibility behavior within the stated algebraic model.

title: Revocable and time-based secure file hierarchy sharing in cloud-assisted internet of things
abstract: Abstract Cloud-assisted Internet of Things (IoT) has been widely accepted for IoT data sharing and outsourcing but owners lose control of their data. Hence, Ciphertext-Policy Attribute-Based Encryption (CP-ABE) is proposed with fine-grained access control for encrypted data. However, a real-world situation exists in which the cloud in the existing schemes may be malicious and with not unlimited resources while data users may access the shared data based on time factor and leave the system dynamically, which can easily lead to data breach leakage, storage exhaustion and privilege confusion. Data auditing, storage saving, user revocation and time-based access control may be a feasible solution to the situation. Therefore, a revocable and time-based file hierarchy CP-ABE scheme is proposed to support user revocation, time-based access control and auditing over hierarchical data, which offers data storage saving and breach detection with efficient access control over dynamic users with time-based sharing requirements. The formal security analysis is presented. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed scheme improves encryption and decryption time by more than $$30\%$$ 30 % and $$50\%$$ 50 % respectively, while its storage saving gains exceeding $$50\%$$ 50 % , confirming its effectiveness and efficiency in complex IoT data sharing scenario.

title: ReasonUni: Reasoning-Augmented Reconstruction Advances Unified Multimodal Models
abstract: Image-to-text (I2T) understanding and text-to-image (T2I) generation are dual tasks in unified multimodal models (UMMs). Reconstructive post-training couples these tasks, but existing reconstruction-based methods remain perception-centric and provide limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation. We propose ReasonUni, a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework that extends this coupling beyond perception. Given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM first reasons about what and how to edit and describes the target state, then generates the corresponding target image conditioned on this understanding output. To jointly optimize both modules, we introduce TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains in both understanding and generation, showing that reasoning-augmented reconstruction yields genuine mutual gains for UMMs.

title: Where Should the Gaussians Go? Reusable Label-Aware Allocation for Budget-Constrained Gaussian Splatting of Cinematic CT
abstract: Anatomical labels help 3D Gaussian splatting preserve vessels in cinematic renderings of CT, but the representation is still found by optimising each patient's scene, where densification decides where Gaussians go, while real-time displays cap their number. We address one part of this process: deciding where a fixed budget of B Gaussians should be placed. We propose a reusable, labelaware allocation front end that maps a patient's CT, labels and transfer function to a density over 2mm cells and draws exactly B positions from it without per-patient optimisation; the other Gaussian attributes are still fitted per patient. The front end is learned once from per-patient optimised scenes and implemented as a population-trained neural prior and an interpretable seven-parameter visibility-aware closed form (VACF). With identical attribute fitting on 20 held-out patients at 10K-100K Gaussians, both raise vessel-masked PSNR over uniform allocation by 4.5-7.1dB and over pruning a dense voxel-aligned model by 1.6-3.3dB. The neural prior does not differ significantly from per-patient optimised allocation at any budget, and VACF is within 0.6dB of it on vessels; on 19 external patients the neural prior again matches it on vessels and VACF is within 0.7dB. As an initialisation for position optimisation, VACF allocation beats per-patient densification on vessels at 10K Gaussians and, at 25K, reaches a higher vessel PSNR after 118s of optimisation than densification after 248s. Under altered rendering presets, VACF transfers to new colours and lighting but not to a label-free transfer function, whereas the neural prior shows the opposite pattern.

title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.

title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
abstract: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.

title: L2G-SR: Learning to Guide LLM-based Symbolic Regression
abstract: Symbolic regression searches for an equation that explains observed data. Numerical error is commonly used to guide the search, but it alone can favor an accurate surrogate over a candidate with the right structure. We propose L2G-SR, a framework for LLM-based symbolic regression that guides search with a learned structural verifier. We construct structural supervision signal using tree edit distance (TED), accounting for commutative operators and alternative expression forms. A verifier first aligns numerical observations with the formulas, then learns to score a candidate's structural similarity to the target formula. At search time, the target formula is hidden and the verifier complements numerical error in parent selection. An analyst then uses verifier feedback and diagnostic tools to propose revisions, which a generator converts into refined expressions. On LLM-SRBench, L2G-SR achieves state-of-the-art numerical fit, equation level accuracy and TED across the evaluated LLM backbones and domains. L2G-SR demonstrates the value of learned structural guidance for LLM-based symbolic regression.

title: International Journal on Information Theory (IJIT)
abstract: A class of binary sequences, constrained with respect to the length of zero runs, is considered.For such sequences, termed (d, k)-sequences, new combinatorial and computational resultsare established. Explicit expressions for enumerating (d, k)-sequences of finite length areobtained. Efficient computational procedures for calculating the capacity of a (d, k)-code aregiven. A simple method for constructing a near-optimal (d, k)-code is proposed. Illustrativenumerical examples demonstrate further the theoretical results.

title: Simulation Framework, Chi-Distribution Validation, and Reconstruction Methods for KLJN Secure Key Exchange
abstract: The Kirchhoff-Law–Johnson-Noise (KLJN) key exchange protocol offers a classical, physics-based alternative to quantum key distribution for achieving informationtheoretic security. It offers a classical and cost-effective solution to secure communications. In this paper we present a simulation framework that models the entire KLJN loop, enabling detailed exploration of the scheme, and propose workflows to generate KLJN key-exchange probability density functions, and to validate their accuracy against analytically calculated ones. We also use our simulation to empirically verify that voltage and current standard deviations of a KLJN scheme follow chi-distributions, a result that crucially impacts threshold optimization and bit-classification algorithms. We also introduce correction techniques that reconstruct the original statistical behavior after signal-processing operations such as windowing and low-pass filtering, which are essential for reducing transients between bit transfers and enhancing security. This work integrates statistical signal analysis, and simulation-driven validation to strengthen the theoretical and practical foundations of KLJN-based secure communication.

title: Quantum authentication framework for digital twin–driven satellite networks
abstract: Abstract The integration of digital twin technology into large-scale Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations introduces critical security challenges, particularly under emerging quantum threats. This paper proposes a quantum-assisted multi-layer authentication framework for satellite–digital twin communication that combines entanglement-based verification with hardware-rooted identity using Quantum Physical Unclonable Functions (QPUFs). The protocol employs Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen (EPR) pair-based key establishment and decoy-state mechanisms to detect entangle-and-measure (EMA) and intercept-and-resend (IRA) attacks, where the induced disturbance attains 0.25 per decoy qubit under a maximally informative attack. The probability of undetected attacks decreases exponentially as $$(3/4)^u$$ , rapidly approaching zero for moderate decoy lengths. Cabello’s qubit efficiency of the scheme is derived as $$\beta = \frac{k}{6n + 2u}$$ . Experimental validation using Qiskit simulation confirms entanglement correlation preservation across mutually unbiased bases and demonstrates QPUF response uniformity of 0.588, a stabilized majority-based reliability of $$100\%$$ under noiseless simulation, and a response uniqueness of 0.508. The results establish the feasibility of integrating quantum authentication and hardware-root security within digital twin–assisted satellite networks.

title: EGCForest: Structured Agent Memory Organization for Enterprise Group Chats
abstract: Enterprise group chats record project progress, decisions, task ownership, and other organizational information valuable to enterprise agents. Reliable retrieval is challenging because evidence spans interleaved threads, channels, and time, with meaning and authority conditioned on the speaker. Neither RAG's independent chunk retrieval nor memory systems' summary-based consolidation can reliably recover such distributed evidence. We present EGCForest, a novel multi-view hierarchical memory framework for enterprise group chats. EGCForest organizes an immutable message log into three complementary forests: a Channel forest for temporal workflows, an Actor forest for speaker-conditioned context, and an Artifact forest for deliverable lifecycles. Cross-view connections are enabled by a Placement Map and sparse structural bridges. Built on this memory backbone, EGCForest retrieves and assembles evidence by jointly leveraging message-level relevance, hierarchical context from forest summaries, and cross-view links, recovering distributed evidence. Experiments on three enterprise-chat benchmarks show that EGCForest consistently outperforms RAG and memory-system baselines, improving answer accuracy by up to 20.85 points over MemOS while supporting efficient online retrieval.

title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.

title: O-RAN-Native Jamming Detection Under Network Heterogeneity
abstract: Radio-frequency jamming threatens cellular network operations in contested environments. The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture exposes per-User Equipment (UE) telemetry through the E2 interface, enabling Key Performance Indicator (KPI)-based jamming detection without proprietary hardware. However, operational deployment demands detection methods that generalize across heterogeneous networks. We propose a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) combining adaptive Median Absolute Deviation (MAD)-based baseline detection, count-based anomaly detection, and abrupt change detection through a weighted voting system. SEM operates in two modes: a cold-start mode requiring no labeled data for immediate deployment, and a supervised mode where parameters are refined offline via grid search as labeled data accumulates. We evaluate SEM against five machine learning (ML) classifiers and five deep learning (DL) sequence models using approximately 25 hours of testbed data comprising logs from eight heterogeneous 5G environments, employing both single-environment and multi-environment leave-one-out (LOO) validation. Our analysis indicates that under conditions not encountered during training (distribution shift), learning-based models tend to lose recall and miss jamming events, whereas SEM, even in cold-start mode, maintains detection capabilities at the cost of false alarms. Furthermore, SEM's parameter optimization can be mapped to O-RAN's Non-RT RIC as an rApp for continuous refinement, allowing operators to transition to learning-based alternatives once corpus coverage is sufficient.

title: PFedMA: Who Should Join Next as Federated Multi-Agent Orchestration Evolves?
abstract: Federated Multi-Agent Systems (FedMAS) offer a promising paradigm for collaborative reasoning among LLM-based agents while keeping raw client data decentralized. However, reliable multi-round collaboration remains challenging. Agent selection must take into consideration evolving task requirements and the agent's historical reliability, while privacy rules must adapt to changing collaboration contexts and meet the client's personalized needs. To address these challenges, we propose PFedMA, a federated multi-agent framework for feedback driven multi-round collaboration under heterogeneous privacy requirements. Across rounds, PFedMA maintains historical capability and reliability states to guide agent selection, evaluates task responses before aggregation, and refines subsequent queries according to accumulated collaboration feedback. PFedMA enables bidirectional local to global and global to local private rule evolution across heterogeneous clients. Clients generalize locally updated privacy rules and selectively incorporate globally maintained rules, thereby facilitating cross-client privacy rule evolution while preserving personalized constraints. Extensive experiments across reasoning, privacy sensitive, and adversarial settings show that PFedMA improves task performance, reduces measured privacy leakage, and improves system robustness.

title: Honest agent scores: do benchmark defects or repeats change which AI agent wins?
abstract: A reproducible check of two common claims about AI agent leaderboards, on 3,300 public Terminal-Bench 4.0 runs (10 configurations, 66 tasks, 5 trials each). Removing the 30 tasks flagged as defective by Epoch AI does not change the ranking beyond noise, and ranking by pass^5 instead of pass@1 does not either. Agents do differ in how correlated their repeats are on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and much of that difference sits in the 28 tasks the benchmark later changed. With 66 tasks, pass@1 differences within about 9.5 points are ties. Every result is recomputed from raw trials by reproduce.py with fixed seeds. Also includes a tool to run the same tests on any leaderboard with per-trial data.

title: СРАВНИТЕЛЬНЫЙ ОБЗОР ИСПОЛЬЗОВАНИЯ РАССУЖДЕНИЙ (REASONING) В БОЛЬШИХ ЯЗЫКОВЫХ МОДЕЛЯХ
abstract: Проведён подробный сравнительный анализ современных подходов к реализации и оценке рассуждений в больших языковых моделях (LLM) — ключевой технологии в области искусственного интеллекта и обработки естественного языка. Рассмотрены и проанализированы методы цепочки рассуждений (Chain-of-Thought, CoT), автоматические цепочки рассуждений (Automatic Chain-of-Thought, Auto-CoT), дерево рассуждений (Tree-of-Thought, ToT) и граф рассуждений (Graph of Thoughts, GoT), а также архитектурные модификации, такие как масштабирование вычислений во время инференса (Test-time Compute), направленные на увеличение вычислительной мощности в процессе генерации ответов. Особое внимание уделено преимуществам и ограничениям каждого из этих методов, а также механизмам их работы внутри архитектуры трансформеров, включая взаимодействие слоёв внимания и MLP-модулей. Подчёркнута важность комплексных и многоступенчатых тестов, которые требуют от моделей не просто извлечения знаний, а настоящего логического вывода и способности к интервенциям, что позволяет повысить качество и надёжность рассуждений. Рассмотрены также современные техники промптинга, такие как обучение с небольшим числом примеров (few-shot) и без примеров (zero-shot CoT), и их влияние на точность решений в различных задачах — от арифметики до контрафактического мышления.

title: When Vowels Don't Help: Empirical Limits of Vowel-Consonant Separation for Compression and LLM Pipelines
abstract: We study a simple linguistic transform that separates English vowels from consonants (MVD, Maharashtran Vowel Disappearance) and ask whether it helps three common goals: reversible representation, lossless compression with standard codecs, and cheaper LLM/RAG pipelines via lossy vowel dropping. The reversible split works. Lossless MVD serialization plus gzip/bz2/zlib is worse than compressing raw text (about -120% relative improvement on short synthetic corpora; still strongly negative on real books). Lossy vowel dropping before gzip does help: about +14% mean savings on synthetic text and +20.5% mean savings on real public-domain prose at >=200 KB. The same lossy transform fails for RAG-relevant proxies: tiktoken (cl100k_base) token counts increase by an unweighted mean of 76.8%, and sentence-transformer cosine similarity collapses to 0.17 (96.7% of pairs below 0.6). We conclude that vowel dropping is a narrow byte-level compression trick, not a path to LLM token or embedding efficiency. Byte savings do not transfer to BPE tokenizers or pretrained embedders that rely on recognizable subword units. Code: Github_MVD

title: Synthetic Hate Speech Data Underrepresents Minority Groups
abstract: The use of synthetic data is becoming increasingly widespread in a variety of applications. For hate speech detection, synthetic data offers the chance to overcome limitations of existing models and datasets, such as data scarcity, negative psychological impact on annotators, and privacy issues. However, previous work on the topic has only focused on evaluating synthetic datasets extrinsically, by measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic texts. In this work, in addition to measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic data in cross-distribution setups, we carry out a qualitative analysis, aiming at assessing how closely synthetic data can mimic authentic user-generated and human-annotated data. We focus in particular on possible issues related to (under)representation of specific minority groups as targets of hate in synthetic data. To do this, we augment an existing English hate speech dataset by paraphrasing the original gold data using three large language models, and then evaluate the synthetic data both quantitatively, including testing out-of-distribution model generalization, and qualitatively, examining the realism of synthetic texts, their hate speech content, and whether they represent the same identity groups as the original data. We pair this analysis with a detailed breakdown, for each demographic characteristic, of how the synthetic data creation process affects the representation of each specific type of identity, which is the main contribution of our work. We find that, while the performance of models trained on synthetic data is promising, these texts are easily identified as written by an LLM by humans, hate speech labels are not necessarily preserved, and the paraphrasing process tends to erase representation of minority groups and intersectional identities, affecting certain demographics more than others.

title: Integrating domain knowledge and user requirements in kitchen layout optimization
abstract: Abstract Layout design data sources exhibit a fundamental asymmetry: the challenge lies in processing structured, high-quality domain knowledge alongside task-specific natural language user requirements. To address this, we propose a hybrid evaluation framework for evolutionary algorithms (EAs) that quantifies constraint violations as virtual displacement costs. The framework is evaluated in the present study on four kitchen-layout optimization scenarios with task-specific user requirements and component sets. By integrating hard-coded domain rules with a fuzzy-logic-driven Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), the system enables a flexible yet explainable scoring mechanism. This approach allows for a granular penalty system for individuals, while also guiding local search heuristics through component-level diagnostic logging. The implementation of the AST results in a marginal reduction in convergence cost while reducing the relative dispersion of the algorithms. Within this kitchen-layout benchmark, the evolutionary algorithms achieved lower execution times and aggregate penalty scores than the selected LLM chat applications. The three non-expert human-generated layouts were included only as an exploratory reference because of the small and demographically homogeneous participant sample.

title: Quantum Partial Information Decompositions, an Operational Order on Ensembles, and Direct Quantifications of Objective Information
abstract: The partial information decomposition (PID) framework is an extension of classical information theory that enables a systematic analysis of the structure of information in multipartite systems. We advance a simple extension of this framework enabling the construction of multipartite quantum PIDs (QPIDs); generalizing recent, exclusively bipartite, extensions. We construct two QPIDs of the Holevo quantity. First a naive QPID based on the classical minimum mutual information. Second a sophisticated QPID enabled by our development of an operational partial order on quantum ensembles in terms of ensemble (inter-)convertability. Finally, as a concrete example of how QPIDs can be applied, we investigate objectivity scenarios; using our Holevo QPIDs to directly quantify objective information in extended graph states. These findings ultimately establish a foundation upon which generic multipartite QPIDs can be systematically constructed, introduce an operational partial order on ensembles, advance QPIDs as interesting objects of study in their own right, and demonstrate their immediate applicability to problems in quantum information.

title: Teaching Agents in their Own Style: Blackbox Teacher Distillation for Web Agents
abstract: Frontier web agents using closed models have high inference and computational costs. Smaller open models can be an alternative, but to be performant, they require training supervision from a human or teacher model. Token-level teacher distillation is not an option for closed teachers as it needs access to the model's logits. The standard approach is to imitate teacher demonstrations offline, but it trains the student on states it has never visited, and in a style it does not write in. We introduce WebKD, where the teacher is the editor of the student's failures. Given a failed episode, the teacher finds the first point of mistake, and rewrites the student's reasoning traces, harness states, and actions from that point onward. The editing reveals that the teacher's corrections can be more surprising to the student than the student's own text. WebKD instead aims to edit minimally. In the data space, the teacher writes each correction in the student's style. In the objective space, the reasoning is weighted by its contribution to the action. A role-asymmetric KL anchor allows the corrected action to move freely while keeping the reasoning near the student's prior. On the TimeWarp benchmark, WebKD students gain about 5.5-10.7 pp over behavior cloning, outcome-reward RL, and teacher editing baselines. The performance transfers to unseen versions and to the live web in the OnlineMind2Web benchmark. WebKD opens a new way of distilling black-box models to improve the capabilities of open-weight web agents.

title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models
abstract: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. It links targets by feature and require/forbid mode, evaluating their instantiated requirements across variants. ReFormBench comprises 5,000 difficulty-screened three-constraint test instances derived from 910 source questions and covering 66 formatting features. TCPR measures complete instruction compliance, while EMCR measures individual and joint correction of targets opposed to the annotated baseline state. Across ten models, EMCR ranges from 34.04% to 64.72%, and the highest three-target correction estimate is 50.02%. Compliance and correction scores yield different model rankings and task-level profiles. A prompting experiment on Qwen3.5-9B improves both metrics, and the catalog covers over 95% of extracted instances on four additional models. ReFormBench makes response-conditioned correction across instruction variants a measurable dimension of format following. The code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ReFormBench/.

evidence.title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models
evidence.abstract: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. It links targets by feature and require/forbid mode, evaluating their instantiated requirements across variants. ReFormBench comprises 5,000 difficulty-screened three-constraint test instances derived from 910 source questions and covering 66 formatting features. TCPR measures complete instruction compliance, while EMCR measures individual and joint correction of targets opposed to the annotated baseline state. Across ten models, EMCR ranges from 34.04% to 64.72%, and the highest three-target correction estimate is 50.02%. Compliance and correction scores yield different model rankings and task-level profiles. A prompting experiment on Qwen3.5-9B improves both metrics, and the catalog covers over 95% of extracted instances on four additional models. title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.

title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation
abstract: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.

title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

title: Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN): An Analysis of Adaptive Action Grids in Decoupled Q-Learning
abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.
