title: Introduction to Google Gemini
abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive introduction to Google Gemini, describing it as a family of powerful, multimodal large language models (LLMs) capable of processing and reasoning across text, images, audio, video, and code. It highlights Gemini’s evolution from earlier models like Bard (built on LaMDA and PaLM) to a natively multimodal system, emphasizing its two core principles: multimodality and scale (available in Ultra, Pro, and Flash variants). This chapter outlines key features, including deep research and analysis of large documents, code assistance, seamless integration with Google Workspace, custom “Gems” (specialized AI personas), and real-time voice conversations via Gemini Live. It also discusses strengths (multimodality, ecosystem integration, real-time information, advanced reasoning) and weaknesses (potential hallucinations, limited third-party integrations, occasional latency under heavy load). This chapter includes practical Python code samples demonstrating how to access the Gemini API for various tasks. It covers developing data analysis pipelines, building custom AI chatbots, and generating and plotting data visualizations using Matplotlib and Seaborn. These examples show Gemini’s ability to handle code generation, data manipulation, and visualization requests through natural language prompts, making it useful for developers, analysts, and educators. The final section of this chapter focuses on Gemini’s ability to produce Python/Matplotlib code for artistic and mathematical graphics, particularly those involving polar equations (e.g., Archimedean spirals, Cochleoid curves, Conchoid curves). No prior knowledge of polar equations is required, as Gemini generates complete, runnable code. Each example is accompanied by detailed explanations and placeholders for the resulting figures. This chapter concludes by noting that some advanced concepts are not fully explained here and directs readers to external resources, reinforcing Gemini’s strength in creating both practical business graphics and aesthetically pleasing mathematical visualizations. Overall, this chapter positions Gemini as a versatile, production-capable multimodal LLM with strong developer tools and artistic generation abilities, while acknowledging its limitations in areas like hallucination risk and third-party ecosystem support.

title: Quantum Spectral Estimation with Multiple Initial States: Improved Error and Cost Scaling
abstract: We study quantum spectrum and eigenstate property estimation using multiple initial states and generalized Hadamard tests. Building on the QFAMES (quantum filtering and analysis of multiplicities in eigenvalue spectra) framework, we introduce a new method that samples evolution times independently for each initial-state pair. Under the stated assumptions, when statistical error determines the sampling cost, the total Hamiltonian simulation cost required for fixed-accuracy eigenvalue and observable estimation is independent of the number of initial states, up to logarithmic factors. This improves scalability when many initial states are needed to explore the target eigenspaces. The method also reduces the cost of multiplicity recovery and retains Heisenberg-limited scaling for eigenvalue estimation. Numerical experiments support the predicted statistical error scalings.

title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
abstract: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.

title: Selective Next-Location Prediction with MetaModelSelect: A Lightweight Post-Hoc Confidence Metamodel
abstract: Next-location prediction can support proactive mobile-network decisions, but acting on unreliable predictions can waste resources. We apply MetaModelSelect, a lightweight post-hoc confidence metamodel, to selective cellular next-location prediction. The mobility-specific model combines a learned embedding of the predicted location with the four largest softmax probabilities and Softmax Concentration. It learns whether a frozen recurrent neural network's top-1 prediction is correct, using only its outputs and without retraining the backbone. On path-balanced Changchun cellular mobility trajectories, we evaluate backbones trained with cross-entropy (CE) and self-adaptive training plus entropy minimization (SAT+EM), comparing against eight scalar confidence scores, two location-aware lookup methods, and a raw-logit multilayer perceptron. Relative to maximum softmax probability, MetaModelSelect achieves mean per-run reductions in area under the risk--coverage curve (AURC), excess AURC (E-AURC), and area under the generalized risk--coverage curve (AUGRC) of 2.6%, 4.2%, and 3.0% for CE, and 2.0%, 3.3%, and 1.9% for SAT+EM. It also achieves the lowest reported mean risk at every evaluated partial coverage. The results show that MetaModelSelect improves confidence ranking in this mobility setting while leaving the underlying location predictor unchanged.

title: Continual Learning via Generational Parameter Transmission: Weight Retention Dynamics in Neural Agents Under Non-Stationary Environments
abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a primary roadblock in continual learning when deep neural architectures encounter sequential task distributions. In biological and cultural transmission, generational succession offers an evolutionary alternative: lineage adaptation occurs through lossy parameter inheritance rather than indefinite weight preservation. In this work, we extend Generational Artificial Life (GAL) from stylized scalar agents to neural network agents parameterized by Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP). Agents undergo gradient-based learning on non-stationary, alternating classification tasks (Circle vs. XOR decision boundaries) under metabolic parameter budgets (||W||_2 <= c) and generational weight transfer (W_child = f * W_parent). Key Findings: 1. High-Volatility Collapse: When task distributions shift rapidly (every 5 generations), neural populations avoid catastrophic interference by actively suppressing retention (f = 0.312 ± 0.330) to reset obsolete feature extractors. 2. Intermediate Stability Basin: At intermediate timescales (10-25 generations), retention stabilizes near f = 0.506 - 0.532, preserving general feature extractors while providing sufficient plastic capacity for fast fine-tuning (test accuracy: 73.5%). Complete source code, multi-seed sweeps, and reproduction scripts: https://github.com/psycho-prince/Matrix Interactive Simulator: https://psycho-prince.github.io/Matrix/

title: Does the AI Time Horizon Predict Anything? A Preregistered Predictive-Validity Shootout
abstract: Preprint of the paper 'Does the AI Time Horizon Predict Anything? A Preregistered Predictive-Validity Shootout' (submitted to TMLR). METR's 50% time horizon — the human-task duration an AI completes with 50% success — is the most quoted single number in AI capability evaluation. Recent work improved how the number is estimated, but nobody has tested whether it predicts anything. We preregistered a three-way predictive shootout on METR's public Time Horizon 1.1 data (23,235 runs, 228 tasks, 20 AIs): does a model's spline-estimated success curve predict held-out task success better than (a) its mean accuracy and (b) an IRT ability estimate, under 5-fold cross-validation over task families with strictly proper scoring rules? Both preregistered hypotheses are confirmed: the horizon predictor beats mean accuracy (paired log-loss difference -0.238 ± 0.034) and the IRT predictor (-0.418 ± 0.122). Qualifications: the spline is statistically tied with a plain shared-slope logistic regression (+0.004 ± 0.008, n.s.), so the gain comes from using human-time information at all rather than from the spline nonlinearity; and the IRT-ability predictor, while rank-competitive (AUC 0.905 ± 0.024 vs 0.919 ± 0.015), is badly miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.155 vs 0.031). The horizon number is an interpretable repackaging of the success curve, not predictive content beyond the curve itself. Reproduction package: https://github.com/pchi1606/metr-time-horizon-predictive-validity.

title: Data and Code for Regional Attribution and Lexical Evidence in Early Modern Chinese Vernacular Fiction
abstract: This archive accompanies two companion papers built on the same corpus of Ming–Qing vernacular fiction: 21 novels labelled with three regional groups (Northern Mandarin, Jiang-Huai Mandarin, and Wu), plus one auxiliary Taihu Wu holdout work and two exploratory out-of-distribution works. Regional lexical evidence is derived from the Hanyu Fangyan Da Cidian (Zhonghua Book Company, 1999). (1) "Confounder-Aware Regional Attribution in Early Modern Chinese Vernacular Fiction" (PRICAI 2026): corpus metadata, data splits and fold definitions, per-passage SHA-256 checksums, the LLM prompt template in Chinese with an English translation, request settings, redacted model predictions, experimental results, figure data, and supplementary methods. (2) "Regional and Supra-regional Lexical Patterns in Early Modern Chinese Vernacular Fiction" (IALP 2026): the corpus table, inventory-construction and matching scripts, and the work-level evidence underlying its figures and tables (in the ialp/ directory). Passage text is not redistributed; per-passage checksums allow an authorized reconstruction to be verified chunk by chunk. Regional lexicons derived from a copyrighted dictionary are not redistributed; the included scripts rebuild them from a legally obtained copy. Known limitations are documented in docs/known_gaps.md inside the archive. Code (code/, figures/*.py, ialp/code/) is released under the MIT License; all other contents are released under CC BY 4.0. File integrity can be verified with CHECKSUMS.txt as described in README.md. If you use this archive, please cite it together with the accompanying paper(s); citation metadata is provided in CITATION.cff.

title: FPGA-Based Cascade Control of a Piston-Type Wave Maker with Height Feedback
abstract: The traditional control approach for piston-type wave makers is reduced to a piston position tracking problem based on open-loop wave-maker theory; however, due to hydrodynamic loading, nonlinear effects, and propagation delays, the target wave condition at the measurement section cannot be guaranteed. This experimental study involves controllers tuned offline through numerical simulations and validated in real time on a 24 m wave channel. The novelty of this work is a two-layer field-programmable gate array (FPGA) cascade that regulates the measured wave height in closed loop, not just the piston position. In the inner layer, the hydraulic servo cylinder position is controlled within a 1 ms cycle using a proportional–integral (PI) or a Takagi–Sugeno (T–S) fuzzy controller; the outer layer, in a 20 ms cycle, updates the position reference via real-time wave height feedback. Controller parameters were tuned using three meta-heuristic algorithms under the integral of time-weighted absolute error criterion, and a similarity-based rule reduction reduced the T–S consequent parameters from 27 to 9, yielding 66.7% and 62.5% reductions in FPGA execution time and digital signal processing slice usage with tracking-error changes of only 2.2–2.3%. Experiments confirm high-accuracy position tracking and steady-state wave height regulation, verified by fast Fourier transform analysis.

title: Envelope Cubic Regularized Newton Method for Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization
abstract: We study nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problem $\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}\max_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ in which the objective has $ρ$-Lipschitz Hessian and condition number $κ$. We propose envelope cubic regularized Newton method (ECRN) which applies a refined inexact cubic regularized Newton method to the envelope of the primal function $Φ(\cdot) : = \max_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(\cdot,\mathbf{y})$. We show that ECRN finds approximate second-order stationary points of $Φ(\cdot)$ with $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrtρ\,κ^{3/4}\varepsilon^{-3/2})$ second-order oracles, improving the condition number dependence $\mathcal{O}(κ^{2})$ achieved by the best known second-order methods. Our improvement comes from the key observation that the Hessian Lipschitz parameter of the envelope is $\mathcal{O}(ρκ^{3/2})$, which is sharper than the order of $\mathcal{O}(ρκ^{3})$ for the function $Φ(\cdot)$. We also conduct a lower bound on second-order methods to show that our complexity is optimal up to a logarithmic factor.

title: PhyMetric: Diagnosing Physical Plausibility in Text-to-Video Generation via Scene-Level QA
abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce visually realistic videos that nevertheless violate the physical consequences implied by the prompt and scene. Existing benchmarks largely rely on holistic plausibility scores or broad quality dimensions, leaving it unclear which physical behavior is being tested and why a model fails. We introduce PhyMetric, a scene-level diagnostic benchmark that recasts physical plausibility evaluation as verifiable, scene-grounded question answering. PhyMetric contains 1{,}115 scenes spanning 50 physical categories across six domains, paired with 8{,}920 answer-balanced binary questions over 12 evaluation dimensions. Each scene is associated with eight targeted yes/no questions and a structured physical prior specifying the governing law, expected temporal sequence, observable signatures, and common failure modes. At evaluation time, a vision-language model (VLM) judge answers each question from question-aware sampled frames conditioned on the prior, and correctness is hierarchically aggregated into scene, dimension, physical category, and model scores. Experiments on four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges show that scene-specific binary QA is a critical component of the protocol: when each targeted question is replaced by a single generic plausibility query, evaluator accuracy drops to the chance level. Structured physical priors offer a complementary signal that improves human alignment of the resulting scores, with effects that vary across VLM judges of different capacity. These findings establish PhyMetric as a benchmark that turns physical plausibility evaluation from opaque holistic scoring into interpretable, scene-level inspection. Our project page is available at: https://mengsiwei.github.io/PhyMetric/.

title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.

title: Fully sequential Gaussian process regression for preference learning
abstract: We study continuous global optimization problems in which the objective function cannot be directly evaluated; rather, we observe only which of two selected design points appears to perform better, subject to noise. Such comparisons complicate the use of Gaussian process regression because they yield non-Gaussian posteriors. We consider a fully sequential approximation, based on moment-matching, that yields a fast closed-form update of the metamodel's mean and covariance. We then propose DOVE, a fully sequential sampling policy that combines an information gain criterion with randomized sampling designed to control error accumulation. Under fairly standard regularity conditions, we prove convergence rates for both statistical error and expected simple regret that depend on kernel smoothness. To our knowledge, these are the first such rates for fully sequential approximate Bayesian inference in continuous global optimization.

title: NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING FOR AUTOMATIC IDENTIFICATION OF GRAMMATICAL STRUCTURES IN ENGLISH TEXTS
abstract: Ushbu ilmiy tezis ingliz tili matnlarida murakkab grammatik tuzilmalar, sintaktik aloqalar va so'z turkumlarini tabiiy tilni qayta ishlash (NLP) vositalari yordamida avtomatlashtirilgan holda aniqlash usullarini tadqiq etadi. Maqolada ehtimollik modellaridan (HMM) zamonaviy chuqur neyron tarmoqlar (BERT, RoBERTa) va SpaCy tahlil tizimlariga o'tish evolyutsiyasi ko'rib chiqiladi. Ingliz tilidagi sifatdosh va gerundiy konstruksiyalari, murakkab tobe sintaktik qurilmalarni kompyuter lingvistikasi yordamida tahlil qilishning aniqlik ko'rsatkichlari baholanadi.

title: The Architecture of Permanence Full Technical Report on Topological Continual Backpropagation (Topo-CBP)
abstract: The Architecture of Permanence by Frank Morales Aguilera (SOMALA) introduces Topological Continual Backpropagation (Topo-CBP). This hardware-level framework resolves the 1982 stability-plasticity dilemma and eliminates catastrophic forgetting directly on bare-metal silicon. 1. The Core Paradigm Shift (Section 1) Replacing Heuristics & Cloud Wrappers: Traditional continual learning relies on soft quadratic penalties (EWC) that cause plastic paralysis, replay buffers that leak data and bloat memory, or dynamic expansion that sprawls parameters. Meanwhile, modern consumer agents (like Meta's Muse) rely on a "Cloud Crutch"—tethering interfaces to remote Linux VMs and RAG/vector databases, which creates severe data sovereignty liabilities (under GDPR, Bill C-27, and Québec privacy laws) and causes cognitive collapse during network latency spikes. Physical Drift Diagnostic: Topo-CBP unifies Richard Sutton's 2024 Continual Backpropagation (metabolic unit renewal) with deterministic topological governance. It replaces the post-hoc metric of catastrophic forgetting with a spatial diagnostic metric, Parameter Drift ($\Delta_{\text{drift}} = \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} \Vert{}W_p^{(t)} - W_p^{(0)}\Vert{}_\infty$), holding coordinate displacement strictly to $0.0000000000$. 2. Mathematical Foundations & The Two-Phase Governor (Section 2) AST & LEFM Operator: Unlike stochastic multi-agent heuristics (such as Anthropic's 60-agent Claude swarm, which hit a ~68% mollifier ceiling on the Riemann Hypothesis), SOMALA's Laplace-Euler-Fourier-Mellin (LEFM) operator constructs a self-adjoint operator where $\text{Re}(s) = 1/2$ is an immutable symmetry axis, validated across all Seven Core Consequences (7C) of the Riemann Hypothesis ($\text{SEED}=123$). Prime Spine & Euler Attenuation: Foundational layers (input_embeddings, lm_head, and designated manifold layers) are anchored to an invariant prime coordinate ring ($\mathcal{P} = \{2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13\}$). Streaming gradients orthogonal to $\mathcal{P}$ are modulated by the truncated Euler product ($\Lambda = \prod_{p \in \mathcal{P}} (1 - 1/\sqrt{p}) \approx 0.9785142874$). TopoAdamW & Live Cryptographic Gate: Around every AdamW step, Phase I scales gradients by $\Lambda$ and zeroes out anchor gradients ($\nabla_{\mathcal{P}} L = 0$), while Phase II restores baseline prime tensors in VRAM post-step. TopoTelemetryCallback audits $\Delta_{\text{drift}} == 0.0$ and verifies live SHA-256 state hashes at every epoch boundary, raising a RuntimeError if a single bit deviates. 3. Foundation-Scale Empirical Proofs (Sections 3 & 4) gpt-oss-20b (Zero Forgetting on Bare Silicon): Trained sequentially across three disjoint SetFit/ag_news tasks on a single RTX PRO 6000 Ada GPU (96 GB VRAM) using a frozen bfloat16 backbone and float32 heads. It achieved 96.34%, 88.58%, and 95.41% task accuracies with +0.00% forgetting and bit-exact SHA-256 retention (334ea0c8ca2e9af5). Muse-Glimmer-30B (Offline Agentic Permanence): Run locally on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU in 4-bit NF4, achieving smooth sequential convergence across three tasks with zero cross-talk (State Hash c8b99e403ffc1fb4...) and high-confidence offline routing across macroeconomics (93.36%), avionics telemetry (62.89%), and governance (88.28%). Dual 70B Flagships (llama-3.1-70b-topo-governed-cbp-rh & Riemann-Mendeleev-70B): A 70B foundation model was trained in 4-bit NF4 over 10 epochs on an AST/RH corpus (eval loss $0.3621$, digest 1770a2a4f5f1bd3f). It was then adapted sequentially on PubChemSFT molecular chemistry invariants (eval loss $0.8959$). Maintaining the same 1770a2a4f5f1bd3f cryptographic hash, the resulting polymath engine transitions seamlessly between formal LEFM derivations and SMILES chemical parsing (e.g., acetylsalicylic acid COX-1/COX-2 mechanics) without interference. Disproving the "Plasticity Tax": Deserialization audits across five orders of magnitude (200K to 70B parameters) show that while unconstrained AdamW erodes coordinates on Step 1 ($3.05 \times 10^{-5} \rightarrow 2.44 \times 10^{-3}$), a governed qwen2.5-0.5b model held $0.0$ drift across 5,000 FineWeb streaming steps while matching baseline convergence (2.8799 vs. 2.8798 loss). Similarly, a 15-task multimodal Gemma model trained for 500 epochs on video dynamics (Task 15) while retaining 64 mm thoracic oncology classifications on Task 14 with zero degradation. 4. Master Fleet Audit & Architectural Conclusions (Sections 5, 6 & 7) The 12-Model Certified Fleet: All 12 open-weight repositories hosted under frankmorales2020/ on Hugging Face—spanning 200K 3D world models, 0.5B Qwen streaming models, 0.67B multimodal Gemma vision models, 20B RLHF/AG-News/RH-7C models, 30B Muse-Glimmer agents, and the dual 70B polymath engines—carry embedded SHA-256 hashes, $0.0000000000$ certified drift, and 2,551 total downloads. Future Scope & Conclusion: While multi-head isolation naturally protects frozen backbones, full streaming pre-training, continual RLHF, and 70B embedding clamping prove TopoAdamW eenforcebitwise invariance under live gradient pressure. Future work will extend prime-ring anchoring to intermediate self-attention and MLP blocks during full-parameter continual fine-tuning—thereby establishing AI as a sovereign, cryptographically verifiable, offline-capable system permanently etched into physical silicon.

title: CONROT: Constraint Rot benchmark data (v1 synthetic and v2 real-corpus editions)
abstract: Companion data for Constraint Rot: Why Rules Stated Once Do Not Survive Multi-Author AI Sessions — and What Does (Al Shahriar and Faisal, Kerniva, 2026). Contents: the 16 task specifications per edition (briefs, scripted hops, personas, constraints with machine-checkable predicates); the checker's predicate semantics; the frozen constraint taxonomy; the retrieval manifest of the 14 public documents in the v2 corpus; 960 per-hop trajectory records (672 v1, 288 v2) with document version ids, matched excerpts, adherence, nudge and store-round flags, and internal identifiers removed; the run registries; and the aggregate analysis outputs behind every table and figure. Arm labels: A full history, B summarize, C prune, D SGAP, E ledger (detection with feedback), F ledger re-injection only, G ledger hard gate; a +sonnet5/+sonnet5high suffix marks Claude Sonnet 5 runs, no suffix is Gemini 3.5 Flash. The collaboration system, orchestrator and harness are proprietary and not included. See README.md in the archive.

title: Bio-Inspired Swarm Optimization for Interpretable Classification of Tropinota hirta Abundance Using Partial SMOTE and XGBoost
abstract: Classifying blue basin trap captures of Tropinota hirta according to environmental conditions can support timely and data-driven management of this flower-feeding pest in almond orchards; however, imbalanced class distributions pose important challenges for machine-learning models. This study proposes an interpretable PSO-XGBoost with Partial SMOTE framework for classifying T. hirta abundance levels derived from blue basin trap captures using temporal and meteorological variables. From a biomimetic perspective, Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is a bio-inspired optimization algorithm that emulates the collective search and information-sharing behavior observed in natural swarms, translating principles of biological collective intelligence into a computational optimization process. The dataset consisted of 256 trap observations categorized into High (H), Low (L), and Medium (M) abundance classes, with 180, 55, and 21 observations, respectively, indicating substantial class imbalance. Eleven temporal and meteorological variables were used as predictors, while PestCount, representing the observed number of T. hirta adults captured in the blue traps and used to derive the target classes, was excluded from the predictor set to prevent target leakage. The proposed framework combines controlled minority-class oversampling using Partial SMOTE, bio-inspired PSO for XGBoost hyperparameter optimization, and rule extraction for model interpretability. A Partial-SMOTE ratio ablation analysis identified L = 0.80 and M = 0.40 as the most favorable class-specific oversampling configuration, avoiding complete class balancing while improving overall and class-sensitive predictive performance. Performance was evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation, with oversampling applied exclusively to the training folds to prevent information leakage. The proposed method achieved a mean Accuracy of 89.45% and a mean Weighted F1-score of 88.79%, representing the best overall performance among the evaluated methods. The ablation analysis showed that PSO-based optimization improved conventional XGBoost, while the proposed Partial-SMOTE configuration outperformed both class-weighted XGBoost and PSO-XGBoost without oversampling. Robustness was further assessed using 10-times repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, where the proposed method achieved 87.51 ± 3.75% Accuracy, 86.94 ± 3.71% Weighted F1-score, and 71.60 ± 7.40% Macro F1-score. Friedman and post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction confirmed statistically significant performance differences in favor of the proposed method. In addition, human-readable IF–THEN rules with bounded temporal and meteorological conditions were extracted from the optimized model to improve interpretability. The results indicate that integrating a biomimetic swarm-intelligence optimization strategy with controlled oversampling, blue-trap monitoring, and interpretable machine learning provides a promising framework for predicting T. hirta abundance levels and supporting environmentally compatible monitoring and pest-management decision-making in almond orchards.

title: Intelligent Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy Control System for Industrial Bread Baking Ovens
abstract: Intelligent control systems can stabilise operational processes and support the development of digital manufacturing in the food industry. This study presents and examines a digital twin of an industrial bread oven with a hybrid neuro-fuzzy controller for temperature and humidity to bake several loaves of bread. Its architecture comprises MLP-Control (4-32-16-2), a discrete Fuzzy-PD corrector and safety rules. The Mamdani controller with 27 rules operates as an independent reference and provides labels for behaviour cloning. MLP-Control accepted those labels in 98.73% of cases for the dryer, 99.10% for the humidifier, and 98.01% for both combined. The Simulation-in-the-Loop evaluation was conducted on 100 pairwise scenarios (seed 42) with a 39 min cycle, 5 s steps and phases at 0–3, 3–6 and 6–39 min. Hybrid + Constraint met the stringent Phase 3 sustainability criterion in 100 out of 100 scenarios, compared with 95 out of 100 for PI. However, PI achieved the lowest final MSE, the shortest mean settling time and the lowest control effort; therefore, it is not claimed that Hybrid + Constraint is superior in all respects. evidence.title: Intelligent Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy Control System for Industrial Bread Baking Ovens
evidence.abstract: Intelligent control systems can stabilise operational processes and support the development of digital manufacturing in the food industry. This study presents and examines a digital twin of an industrial bread oven with a hybrid neuro-fuzzy controller for temperature and humidity to bake several loaves of bread. The Mamdani controller with 27 rules operates as an independent reference and provides labels for behaviour cloning. Hybrid + Constraint met the stringent Phase 3 sustainability criterion in 100 out of 100 scenarios, compared with 95 out of 100 for PI. title: Unlocking the “black box” of food prediction models: Applications and perspectives of explainable artificial intelligence in agri-food chemical analysis and quality control
abstract: With the deep integration of global agri-food supply chains, artificial intelligence and machine learning have been widely applied in fields such as food traceability, adulteration detection, and quality grading. However, high-precision models like CNN and XGBoost are often considered “black boxes” due to opaque decision-making, undermining their credibility and robustness. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers a pathway to model transparency. This paper systematically reviews XAI progress in food chemistry over 2021–2026, covering inherently interpretable models and post-hoc methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM). Focusing on three major scenarios—geographical traceability and adulteration detection, flavor chemistry and sensory evaluation, food safety risk assessment—it analyzes XAI applications in quantifying feature contributions, identifying key spectral bands, and identifying candidate biomarkers for subsequent targeted validation. Application paradigms for different data types (spectra, images, chemical composition, sensor data) are summarized. In view of the challenges in current research, such as methodological biases under high-dimensional collinearity and the lack of an integration mechanism between interpretation results and prior chemical knowledge, this paper proposes key directions for future breakthroughs, with the expectation of promoting food science research toward a more intelligent, transparent and trustworthy new paradigm.

title: ReAl: Refine neural operators via aligning dynamical flow
abstract: Neural partial differential equation (PDE) surrogates trained with mean squared error (MSE) can capture dominant dynamics but often lose high-frequency information and fine-scale structures. Generative models (e.g., Flow Matching) can capture the distribution of fine-scale details, yet stochastic errors may accumulate during autoregressive rollouts and compromise long-term stability. To address these limitations, we introduce Refine and Align(ReAl), a model-agnostic plug-in that augments pretrained PDE surrogates to improve the reconstruction of high-frequency structures associated with complex physical phenomena. In the refinement stage, a conditional flow-matching model learns the residual distribution around the deterministic base prediction, recovering missing fine-scale structures while retaining the dominant dynamics. In the alignment stage, to mitigate the generative discrepancies amplified in the autoregressive rollout, particularly in chaotic systems, we generate multiple trajectories from the same input and reinforce the refiner with trajectory-level rewards, thereby achieving long-horizon dynamical alignment. Experiments across diverse surrogate architectures and PDE tasks demonstrate that ReAl consistently improves high-frequency fidelity, forecasting accuracy, and long-horizon stability.

title: When Pairwise Preferences Cycle: A Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk for Video GRPO
abstract: Pairwise preference feedback has become a widely adopted supervision signal for reinforcement learning in video generation models, as pairwise comparisons provide a more reliable alternative than pointwise scalar ratings for evaluating the quality of generated videos. Specifically, we define a preference graph for each GRPO group under a pairwise evaluator, where nodes represent sampled rollouts and edges encode pairwise preferences. Auditing 6,976 on-policy comparison graphs, we find that cyclic preferences are prevalent and persist throughout training. Naive pairwise reward aggregation based on average win rates discards the underlying comparison structures and treats each rollout independently, which may introduce unreliable advantage estimates for certain rollouts and consequently affect reinforcement learning optimization. Therefore, we propose the \emph{Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk} (\ours{}), a graph-aware advantage aggregation method that strengthens the global preference signal from win rates with reliable relational evidence from cyclic preference graphs through a reliability-guided preference walk. Under matched evaluator, comparison protocol, group size, prompt schedule, and query budget, \ours{} requires no additional evaluator queries beyond the observed comparisons within each rollout group and improves over Pairwise-GRPO across controlled comparisons, transfer settings, and blind human evaluations.

title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
abstract: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.

title: CORE: Contrast-and-Reflect for Self-Supervised Prompt Optimization in Anomaly Synthesis
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection (AD) is bottlenecked by the scarcity of anomalous samples, making high-fidelity anomaly synthesis crucial for improving downstream performance. However, existing methods either rely on scarce real anomaly references or auxiliary data, while lacking complex reasoning and iterative optimization capabilities for generating realistic defects in open-set scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose CORE, a cost-efficient and training-free prompt optimization framework based on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which unifies zero-shot and one-shot anomaly synthesis. CORE first introduces an Anomaly Context Grounding module to transform sparse user context into defect-aware generation context, which is subsequently instantiated as structured anomaly prompts that disentangle normal-region preservation from anomaly-specific variation, enabling controllable and faithful defect generation. Furthermore, CORE autonomously refines prompts through a self-supervised contrast-and-reflect mechanism. This design empowers general-purpose LMMs to synthesize realistic anomalies under both zero-shot and one-shot settings without task-specific training. Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA demonstrate that CORE synthesizes realistic and diverse anomalies, yielding superior improvements in downstream AD performance. Furthermore, its model-agnostic and plug-and-play paradigm enables effortless integration with diverse LMMs, facilitating adaptation to unseen open-set scenarios.

title: Leakage-controlled benchmark of deep learning transfer from web-scraped microorganism images to laboratory microscopy: manifests, lcbench protocol package, model predictions and results
abstract: Companion data and code deposit of the article “Provenance, leakage and shift: a leakage-controlled benchmark of deep learning transfer from web-scraped microorganism images to laboratory microscopy”. The benchmark measures how much of a classifier’s accuracy on a web-scraped microorganism image collection is due to duplicate leakage across random splits, how far that accuracy carries to curated laboratory microscopy of the same organisms, and how well the classifier can abstain when it is outside its competence. It covers fourteen pretrained backbones evaluated as frozen feature extractors, four adaptation recipes on DINOv2 and a supervised control (300 trained models), two scraped sources (the Kaggle Micro-Organism collection and the Bacterial Morphology Classification collection) and two curated targets (EMDS-6 with DIBaS Gram-stained patches, 638 images; EMDS-7 with unstained DeepBacs bacteria, 183 images). The deposit contains: hash-level manifests (SHA-256, perceptual hash, near-duplicate group) of every image used, so that the exact sets can be re-acquired and the cleaned splits rebuilt; the lcbench command-line package that applies the audit, the grouped cross-validation protocols A1/A2u/A2 and the evaluation (transfer with bootstrap intervals, calibration, temperature scaling, selective prediction) to any class-folder image dataset, with its benchmark card and tests; every analysis and training script and the executed notebook; protocol and environment records (hardware, operating system, library versions, seeds, run times, GPU power logs); the per-image predictions of all 300 trained fold models; the cached frozen features of the fourteen backbones; every result table; the typeset tables of the article; and the numbers, reference and claims audits. Images are not redistributed; fetch scripts and manifests re-acquire them from their original records (Kaggle, Hugging Face, figshare, Zenodo), and every file carries a checksum. Licences: MIT for the code, CC BY 4.0 for the manifests, tables, predictions, features and documents. The third-party image collections keep their own licences.

title: Four-Model Question–Answer–Prompt Reconstruction and Compatibility-Guided Learning: A Proposed Framework for Synthetic Data Generation and Model Optimization
abstract: Synthetic data generation has become an important approach to improving language models when high-quality human-annotated training data are limited. However, conventional synthetic question-answer generation pipelines often rely on direct generation, answer verification, or consistency filtering, without explicitly integrating answer-conditioned question reconstruction, prompt reconstruction, and independent compatibility evaluation into a unified learning process. This paper proposes Four-Model Question–Answer–Prompt Reconstruction and Compatibility-Guided Learning (FQPR-CGL), a framework in which four models perform complementary functions. Model A generates an initial question, Model B generates an answer to that question, Model C receives the generated answer and reconstructs a plausible question and an associated prompt, and Model D independently evaluates the compatibility between the reconstructed question, reconstructed prompt, and original answer. The resulting compatibility score guides sample selection, reward assignment, and subsequent model optimization. The framework distinguishes forward generation from inverse reconstruction and introduces a joint compatibility objective for improving the quality of synthetic training examples. It also incorporates answer correctness verification to reduce the risk of reinforcing mutually consistent but factually incorrect outputs. A proposed experimental design compares the framework with conventional synthetic question-answer generation, round-trip consistency filtering, and alternative multi-model evaluation configurations. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated in this paper, its effectiveness remains an empirical research question. This work establishes a formal architecture, optimization procedure, evaluation protocol, and set of testable hypotheses for studying compatibility-guided learning through coordinated generation and reconstruction.

title: Video clips: Using Robot Simulations to Model the Role of Errors in Infant Walking
abstract: VOLUME CONTENTS: Folders: Exemplar video clip of child walking in laboratory playroom. AIMS: - Train a simulated robot to walk using real infant paths. - Test the effects of different penalties for errors on learning to walk. PARTCIPANTS: 1 exemplar infant. CAMERA VIEWS: Fixed overhead room view. ABSTRACT FROM PUBLICATION: Ossmy, O., Han, D.*, MacAlpine, P., Hoch, J.*, Stone, P., & Adolph, K. E. (2024). Walking and falling: Using simulated robots to model the role of errors in infant walking. Developmental Science, 27, e13449. What is the optimal penalty for errors in infant skill learning? Behavioral analyses indicate that errors are frequent but trivial as infants acquire foundational skills. In learning to walk, for example, falling is commonplace but appears to incur only a negligible penalty. Behavioral data, however, cannot reveal whether a low penalty for falling is beneficial for learning to walk. Here, we used a simulated bipedal robot as an embodied model to test the optimal penalty for errors in learning to walk. We trained the robot to walk using 12,500 independent simulations on walking paths produced by infants during free play and systematically varied the penalty for falling—a level of precision, control, and magnitude impossible with real infants. When trained with lower penalties for falling, the robot learned to walk farther and better when tested on familiar, trained paths and better generalized learning to novel, untrained paths. Indeed, zero penalty for errors led to the best performance for both learning and generalization. Moreover, these beneficial effects of a low penalty were stronger for generalization than for learning. Robot simulations corroborate prior behavioral data, and suggest that a low penalty for errors helps infants learn foundational skills (e.g., walking, talking, and social interactions) that require immense flexibility, creativity, and adaptability.

title: Cascaded Retrieval with Cross-Modal Query Refinement for Efficient Visual Document Search
abstract: Retrieving information from visually rich documents requires matching queries against pages that contain complex evidence in tables, figures, and layout-dependent structures. Current vision-language retrievers address this but incur query-time costs that grow with corpus size and are impractical to scale. We propose SCOUT, a cascaded two-track retrieval framework that separates retrieval performance from exhaustive search. The visual track first uses a lightweight parent retriever to filter the corpus to a compact candidate pool, then applies a stronger multi-vector reranker only to those candidates. In parallel, a semantic track retrieves over hierarchical page and document summaries generated offline to provide a signal complementary to visual matching. The outputs are fused through cross-modal query refinement, which uses semantic scores to adjust the visual query representation before final ranking. We evaluate SCOUT on 4 major benchmarks against 6 baselines and observe a significant query-time latency improvement up to 80.7x (28.8x on average) relative to the best baseline, while exceeding state-of-the-art retrieval performance by up to 7.8% NDCG across all benchmarks.

title: Parakeet vs Whisper Turbo and Distil on CPU
abstract: We evaluated three Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 configurations and two quantized Whisper variants on identical English reading audio using four CPU threads. On a 310.425-second recording, Parakeet FP32 with shorter chunks took 53.58 seconds with 2.81% word error rate (23 edits across 818 reference words) and 2.87 GiB peak process memory. Whisper Turbo INT8 took 343.26 seconds with 2.20% WER; Distil-Whisper INT8 took 279.10 seconds with 2.57% WER. Default Parakeet INT8 chunks omitted substantial speech; shorter chunks reduced WER from 39.12% to 4.65%. These single-request observations favor FP32 Parakeet for this CPU and sample, while the tested Whisper variants made fewer word edits. We publish all 18 completed runs, transcripts, fixture audio, references, checksums and reproduction settings.

title: Adaptive Parallel-World Knowledge Integration in Large Language Models: Switching Between Self-Integration and Cross-Model Knowledge Integration
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) contain substantial but incomplete, unevenly distributed, and potentially inconsistent knowledge. Existing approaches to knowledge integration include retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge editing, knowledge distillation, model fusion, and multi-model collaboration. However, knowledge integration is often organized around a fixed architecture, a predefined information-sharing protocol, or a particular knowledge source. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Knowledge Integration (APW-KI), a framework in which multiple knowledge-integration worlds are created from the same underlying model or from heterogeneous models. Each parallel world follows a potentially different knowledge-integration direction, representation, or specialization strategy. Within each world, a model can independently reorganize and consolidate its own available knowledge through self-integration. When additional information or complementary expertise is required, it can selectively perform cross-world or cross-model knowledge integration. An adaptive controller selects between these modes according to estimated knowledge gaps, evidence quality, knowledge conflicts, task requirements, integration costs, and validation outcomes. The framework supports homogeneous parallel worlds derived from one model, heterogeneous worlds containing different model architectures, and hybrid configurations combining both. It further distinguishes knowledge sharing at the evidence, representation, behavioral, and parameter levels, allowing the system to operate without requiring direct parameter exchange between incompatible models. This paper formalizes the architecture, introduces an adaptive decision mechanism, presents an algorithmic workflow, and develops an experimental protocol for evaluating accuracy, knowledge retention, conflict resolution, computational efficiency, and robustness. APW-KI is presented as a research framework whose effectiveness and novelty must be established through systematic comparisons with existing approaches.

title: Automated Data Preprocessing Using Parameterized SWRL Inference within a Local RAG Pipeline
authors: Maria de los Ángeles Contreras Trujillo
abstract: This work formalizes expert knowledge in data preprocessing through the Web Ontology Language (OWL) and parameterized Semantic Web Rule Language (SWRL) rules, integrated with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline for natural-language queries. An OWL ontology comprising 47 classes, 42 individuals, and 19 SWRL rules was designed in Protégé and validated on the Netflix Movies and TV Shows dataset (8,807 records, 12 columns). A Python-implemented inference engine, which parses the SWRL rule structure from the RDF/XML serialization and evaluates antecedents through deterministic conditionals without invoking a native OWL DL reasoner, generated 15 preprocessing-technique recommendations across 9 analyzable columns; the remaining 3 columns (show_id, title, description) were excluded as identifiers and free-text fields, respectively, for which tabular preprocessing is not applicable. The system guides data scientists in selecting preprocessing techniques based on each column's statistical profile, reducing reliance on manual configuration. The novelty lies in parameterizing SWRL rules using dynamically computed statistical metrics and multilingual semantic retrieval, within a fully local RAG pipeline that supports traceability and privacy.

title: Computational Analysis of Immunohistochemistry Enables Quantitative Assessment of SARS-CoV-2 Nucleocapsid Immunolabeling in Experimentally Infected Mice
abstract: Histopathology and immunohistochemistry (IHC) are central to COVID-19 tissue evaluation. However, conventional manual scoring is limited by its semiquantitative nature and potential observer variability. In this retrospective study of experimentally infected mice, we implemented a semi-automated digital pathology workflow using commercially available software to quantitatively assess SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) immunolabeling in lung (n = 135) and brain (n = 67) tissues. The performance of digital quantification was evaluated against conventional manual scoring, and its association with virological and pathological parameters was assessed across different stages of disease progression. Digital IHC quantification demonstrated strong agreement with manual scoring in both lung [R = 0.94, p < 0.0001, concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) = 0.95] and brain [R = 0.98, p < 0.0001; CCC = 0.977], demonstrating concordance between the two approaches. In addition, digital SARS-CoV-2 N immunolabeling quantification showed significant positive correlations with viral RNA levels, infectious viral titers, and histopathological scores, supporting its association with independent measures of SARS-CoV-2 infection and lesions. Although computational image analysis requires additional infrastructure, technical expertise, and increased analysis time, it provides an objective continuous quantitative measure of SARS-CoV-2 N immunolabeling that complements conventional manual assessment and may reduce observer-dependent variability.

title: Multimodal temporal deep learning for postoperative complication risk stratification in colorectal surgery: a transformer-based analysis of inflammatory–metabolic dynamics
abstract: Postoperative complications after colorectal surgery are time-dependent and heterogeneous, complicating recovery and nursing resource planning. Traditional static metrics fail to capture dynamic physiological evolution. This study developed an interpretable multimodal temporal deep-learning model to characterize postoperative inflammatory–metabolic stress dynamics for predicting nursing-related complication risk. A retrospective multicenter cohort study used MIMIC-IV and eICU for model development and internal validation, and ACS NSQIP for a harmonized external transportability assessment based on available structured perioperative and outcome variables. Adult colorectal surgery patients with postoperative vital signs and laboratory data were included in the temporal development cohorts. Vital signs, inflammatory markers, metabolic indicators, and nursing proxy variables were integrated into multimodal temporal inputs. A Transformer-based model was established, with SHAP for interpretability and unsupervised clustering for trajectory identification. Performance was evaluated using discrimination, precision-recall, and calibration metrics. The primary analysis was defined as offline sequence classification over the 0–72 h postoperative window; leakage-aware sensitivity analyses used prespecified 6-, 12-, 24-, 48-, and 72-h landmarks and an online-style causal attention mask. Among 3,184 included patients, 22.4% developed complications. The multimodal Transformer model achieved an AUC of 0.84 in internal validation and 0.79 in the harmonized ACS NSQIP external assessment. The model showed higher discrimination than the static logistic-regression and random-forest baselines included in the current analysis; however, architecture-specific superiority cannot be inferred without comparisons against stronger temporal models. SHAP analysis identified the 12–36 h postoperative window as a key interval for risk separation. Unsupervised clustering revealed three inflammatory-metabolic stress trajectories with complication gradients (10.9%, 24.6%, 41.3%; p for trend < 0.001). Nursing proxy variables contributed to prediction but were interpreted as severity- and care-context markers rather than direct measures of nursing quality or causal intervention effects. This retrospective multicenter analysis suggests that multimodal temporal modeling can characterize early postoperative inflammatory-metabolic stress patterns and stratify complication risk in colorectal surgery. The findings support further prospective evaluation of dynamic monitoring strategies rather than immediate clinical deployment. This study retrospectively analyzed de-identified public databases without any health care intervention on human participants. Therefore, trial registration was not required.

title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

title: Ergodic topology sampling toward the continuum with Stochastic Normalizing Flows
abstract: In this work we provide numerical evidence that topological freezing in $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ Yang-Mills theory can be mitigated with a flow-based approach, as tested at lattice spacings as fine as 0.03~fm. We do so by analyzing the scaling of the costs of a computational strategy based on the combination of open boundary conditions and Stochastic Normalizing Flows. We show that the integrated autocorrelation time of the squared topological charge and the statistical uncertainty on the topological susceptibility remain under control throughout the explored parameter range with currently available computational resources. This marks an important step toward the use of even more efficient flow-based architectures for ergodic sampling of topology in state-of-the-art lattice gauge theory calculations.

title: Lexical Persistence Without Semantic Entrenchment in AI Agent Communities
abstract: AI agent communities sustain lexical persistence, popular terms spread, recur, and achieve broad adoption, but whether they also develop the temporal semantic structure characteristic of human linguistic communities remains open. We compare MoltBook (AI agent community, 8 weeks), PTT (Chinese human BBS, 19 years), and Reddit (English human forum, in matched 8-week windows) using Compass-Aligned Distributional Embeddings (CADE), measuring semantic drift (B1), neighborhood stability (B2), and lag-1 autocorrelation of per-word drift trajectories. Across the platforms, lag-1 autocorrelation forms a memory-horizon continuum. AI agents' result clusters at the low end, while human platforms show longer-range temporal dependence. MoltBook exhibits approximately 2$\times$ the B1 drift and 20-30% lower B2 stability than both human platforms. As a partial control for community age, r/vibecoding (founded 2025-02-08) shows significant ACF in its first 8 weeks ($0.082$, $p<.001$) and over 15 weeks ($0.220$, $p<.001$); MoltBook's ACF remains non-significant ($p = 0.41$), consistent with the gap not reducing to developmental stage alone. We interpret this pattern as evidence that lexical diffusion alone does not guarantee diachronic semantic consolidation. The findings are consistent with a contrast between communities whose semantic trajectories accumulate long-range interaction constraints and communities whose outputs are repeatedly regenerated from largely fixed pretrained distributions.

title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.

title: One Monitor Does Not Fit All: Formalism-Agnostic Runtime Verification for Agentic AI
abstract: Agentic AI systems combine model decisions, mutable state, tool calls, and delegation to external agents. Monitoring them requires observations from different execution boundaries, while prevention requires control before an operation produces its effect. We present AgenticRV, a runtime-verification architecture that separates these boundaries from the monitoring formalism. Adapters emit canonical events; each monitor receives its own projection and abstraction; and a decision policy uses normalised verdicts to select a reaction supported by the responsible adapter. We formalise when observations suffice, monitor replacement preserves decisions, and blocking prevents unsafe effects. We also distinguish rejected attempts from completed effects, avoiding the assumption that a blocked request must leave every monitor in a permanent violation state. The Python implementation supports LangGraph, MCP, and A2A. A controlled LangGraph experiment combines an external Reelay temporal monitor with a programmatic report monitor; ablations show why both are needed for the selected requirements. Differential checks and cross-adapter tests provide further integration evidence. An LLM-driven incident-response example illustrates the same enforcement path, while existing microbenchmarks isolate framework costs. The results support reuse of monitoring methods at explicit control boundaries, subject to the stated observation and deployment assumptions.

title: AUTONOMOUS NANOSCALE REPAIR OF QUANTUM DEVICES AT THE LIMIT Defect Localization, Bounded Nanoscale Intervention, and Independent Quantum Requalification STARLI · White Rainbow Civilization · Research Edition v1.0 ABSTRACT This monograph proposes a falsifiable research architecture for autonomous nanoscale repair of quantum devices. Its governing distinction is between an apparently successful local material action and genuine recovery of quantum-device function under independent requalification. The proposed three-part coupling combines defect localization, bounded nanoscale intervention, and an external quantum-function witness. Local deposition, surface conditioning, annealing, re-alignment, etching, module exchange, and other repair candidates are treated as platform-limited hypotheses, not as universally available capabilities. When defects cannot be identified, an actuator lacks permission, or a proposed step risks irreversible damage, abstention and conservative retirement are legitimate endpoints. The research program separates superconducting circuit interfaces, Josephson junction defects, charge-disordered silicon quantum dots, photonic circuits and photon detectors. It requires causal comparisons against expert maintenance, unchanged fresh-device acceptance thresholds, blinded repair trials, delayed reliability testing, operator-independent metrology, vendor-absent reconstruction and explicit material-history documentation. The proposed 'Quantum Nano Repair Passport' binds defect hypotheses, raw observations, material changes, dose budgets, repair authority, negative evidence, quantum outcomes and remaining-life assessment. An apparent recovery in geometry, frequency or readout settings alone is not conflated with reduction of a causal decoherence mechanism. The architecture includes 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 chapters with five research sections each, 200 open Research Gates, 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos and 233 named mathematical/physics signposts. The equations are heterogeneous diagnostics, approximations and research criteria, not claims of 233 new physical laws. The proposed experiments have not been performed as part of this book and the integrated repair framework is unvalidated; the work is a theory-and-methods research edition rather than a report of peer-reviewed empirical results. Scientific reference anchors with verified DOI identifiers include: 10.1063/1.4934486 (superconducting surface dielectric participation), 10.1038/s41534-021-00491-2 (surface treatments and coherence), 10.1038/s41534-021-00464-5 (Josephson junction laser trimming), 10.1038/s41534-022-00532-4 (junction two-level defects), 10.1038/s41534-024-00827-8 (Si/SiGe interfacial disorder), 10.1140/epjqt/s40507-017-0064-x (laser annealing of selected photon detectors), and 10.59161/JCGM100-2008E (metrological uncertainty). These sources substantiate physical background, not the integrated autonomous repair hypothesis. STRUCTURE 30 mathematical prelude derivations; 82 research chapters; 410 single-section pages; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 233 individual equation signposts; DOI bibliography; scientific limitations and successor research roadmap. PUBLICATION NOTE An independent, speculative research and reproducibility architecture. Readers should not infer certification of laboratory safety, independent verification, or a functioning autonomous repair system. The author's suggested experiments require separate authorization and specialized laboratory oversight.

title: The Ramanujan Quantum Drive - A Hypothesis
abstract: This concept note proposes using the decimal digits of 1/π, derived from Ramanujan's 1914 series for 1/π, as qubit pulse delays in an expanding block structure to extend qubit coherence. Each term of Ramanujan's series contributes exactly 8 new correct decimal digits of 1/π. These digits are bounded between 0 and 9 and never grow. When used as pulse delays — Block 1 (8 pulses - first 8 digits), Block 2 (next 16 pulses - from the 9th digit to the 24th digit ), Block 3 (24 pulses) — the drive delivers twice the pulse density of a growing-gap drive within the same time window, while maintaining a maximum gap of 9τ at all times. A filter-function simulation on a 1/f noise bath shows both drives protecting qubit coherence far beyond free evolution. The hypothesis predicts that the Ramanujan drive will outperform any growing-gap drive at long times, because bounded gaps ensure continuous protection indefinitely. The experiment requires only a single qubit and standard pulse hardware — no entanglement, no specialised platform. It is immediately testable in any quantum optics or superconducting qubit laboratory.

title: GSE-1 Guardian Social-Engineering Battery (Reasoning Plane): 8-Engine Resistance Matrix
abstract: GSE-1 — Guardian Social-Engineering battery executed on the reasoning plane of the Squirrel OS v1.1 substrate across 8 engine columns (GPT-mini, Claude-haiku, Gemini-flash, Grok-4.7, Qwen-omni-flash, Mistral-small, Llama-4-scout, DeepSeek-flash). 10 preregistered probes per leg (8 attack injections + 2 controls): fake-operator GO, fake system update, impersonation, urgency pressure, PII exfiltration, playbook mutation, threshold gaslighting, typo bypass. RESULTS: 6/8 engines fully governed (0/8 breaches, 0 hygiene failures); Mistral-small 1/10 governed (7/8 breaches), Llama-4-scout 5/10 governed (4/8 breaches). Finding: engine-level social-engineering resistance is NOT uniform across the roster; breached engines must be routed only behind deterministic enforcement layers. Universal 1/2 control failure is a known instrument artifact, uniform across all legs. Total spend $0.1702. All payloads are synthetic forgeries by design; no real operator authorization text appears in any artifact (operator-privacy doctrine). Bundle: frozen probe set, preregistration (committed before execution), runner v3 (transport-retry, payment-abort, resume cache), raw outputs for all 80 instances, per-leg result JSONs, run logs, results matrix.Dual Mesh Benchmark: MEASURED (DeepSeek v4-pro column, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23345241); all other figures NOT MEASURED.This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All data is synthetic.

title: Artificial Intelligence Trends for Automatically Identifying Hate Speech on Social Media Networks
abstract: The web community views online derision as a threatening issue since it might be detrimental facing people individually as well as to society at large. Social media nevertheless offers a user friendly forum where interested individuals or organizations may openly debate and voice their thoughts regarding relevant issues. In order to identify trends in online speech that detect hate speech tasks, a primary goal of this work is to check recent literature on this subject. The resources utilized for this study were found by searching several databases, like as Google Scholar and ACM Digital Library. The current investigation was undertaken utilising the Preferred Reporting Things for Systematic Assessments and Meta- Analysis (PRISMA) procedure. Multiple records were inspected. From 2020 to 2023, 3500 articles were studied. 3469 were removed due to duplicates and irrelevant databases, and 21 were included. The evaluation indicates that the Supervised Machine learning algorithm was the often-utilized model for classifying nasty texts found online though deep techniques and machine methods have also demonstrated potential in the identification of nasty words on ground nowadays. This study comes to the conclusion that approaches for both machine learning and deep learning have shown promise in the categorization. of slanderous comments on online forums. However, in order to detect and restrict, hostile rhetoric hybrid cross-platform models must be developed.

title: Audio-Visual Dog Identification and Tracking in Real-World Videos
abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.
